newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire war rivals to meet in last chance for peace.
newsitem.headline: Zaire war rivals to meet in last chance for peace.

text.p: Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila meet on a ship off Congo on Wednesday with hosts South Africa optimistic they can avert a bloody battle for the capital Kinshasa.

With Kabila insisting, in public at least, that Mobutu hand over power at the meeting, South African officials confirmed that both men would join President Nelson Mandela on the ship at Congo's port of Pointe Noire.
Zaire's capital Kinshasa, which Kabila has threatened to take by force if Mobutu refuses to go, spent its first night of the war under curfew.
"President Mandela and Deputy President (Thabo) Mbeki are both quite optimistic that an agreement can be reached on Wednesday," Mandela's spokesman Joel Netshitenzhe said in South Africa.

He said agreement had been reached by telephone on Tuesday on the framework for an accord. "They have a skeleton of the main areas of agreement that are supposed to be ratified tomorrow," he told Reuters.
U.S. special envoy Bill Richardson, who helped bring Mobutu and Kabila together for an inconclusive meeting on the ship on May 4, shared the South African optimism.

"I am optimistic that there will be a soft landing and a peaceful, inclusive transition, mainly because of South Africa's very strong and effective and skilful efforts," he told reporters at the United Nations in New York.
Mobutu, 66, has cancer. He has dominated Africa's third largest country since seizing power in 1965.
The rebels, who took up arms in October demanding Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, control three-quarters of Zaire.
Kabila and his spokesmen have said throughout the peace talks that Mobutu must hand power to them. They have ruled out a transfer of power to any other transitional authority.
Reports reaching Kinshasa said the rebels had taken the key bridge over the River Kwango and Zaire's armed forces (FAZ) had pulled back to Mbankana about 150 km (100 miles) from the city.

Information Minister Kin-Kiey Mulumba told Reuters he could make no immediate comment on the reports. On Monday, he told reporters there was fierce fighting in the region of Kenge, 60 km (40 miles) to the east of the bridge.
Kabila's son Joseph, a frontline commander, has said that the rebels are advancing on all fronts.
Kinshasa's usually bustling streets emptied after the curfew took effect at 8 p.m. Families sat out on their balconies, speculating about what might happen. The curfew ends at 6 a.m.

France, among Western powers with troops in neighbouring Congo to evacuate foreign nationals if need be, accused the Tutsi-dominated rebels of slaughtering Rwandan Hutu refugees after taking the town of Mbandaka on Tuesday.
"France condemns these criminal acts," its foreign ministry said. Mbandaka is some 600 km (370 miles) northeast of Kinshasa by river.
